newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope's operation puts spotlight on his frailty.
newsitem.headline: Pope's operation puts spotlight on his frailty.

text.p: Pope John Paul, who was entering hospital on Sunday to have his appendix removed, has had a chequered health history during his 18-year-old papacy.
He went from a robust globetrotter in the early days of his papacy to a frail, tired and pained figure in his later years.
In the past two years, the health of the 76-year-old Pope has declined noticeably and a trembling left hand has become more and more uncontrollable.
Doctors viewing him from a distance attribute the shaking hand, rigidity of the facial muscles and a slow, stooped gait to Parkinson's Disease or a related neurological disorder.
His ability to recover from accidents and illnesses for most of his life has been attributed to his love of physical activity as a young man, a priest and bishop.
Karol Wojtyla's first health crisis as Pope came three years after his election. On May 13, 1981, Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca shot him during an audience in St Peter's Square.
He nearly died from wounds to the stomach and hand and Agca's bullets came within a hair of hitting vital organs.
Doctors operating furiously for five hours saved his life at Rome's Gemelli hospital, the same Catholic institution where he is to undergo the appendectomy.

John Paul was released less than two weeks later but had to re-enter the hospital for a virus infection contracted by blood transfusions during the first surgery and to have a temporary excluding colostomy reversed.
History's most travelled Pope, he was back on the road nine months later with a gruelling trip to four African countries.
For the next decade he enjoyed near-perfect health.
In July 1992, when he was 72, the Pope entered hospital for removal of a large intestinal tumour the size of an orange. The tumour was caught when it was beginning to turn malignant.
During that operation doctors also removed his gall bladder when they found it to contain many stones. Lymph nodes were also removed in case the tumour had already started to spread.

His personal doctor, Renato Buzzonetti, came under intense media criticism for not having detected the tumour earlier. But the Vatican said the Pope had shown no symptoms until several weeks before the operation.
It was the start of a spate of health problems.
In November 1993, the Pope fell down the stairs of his throne during a Vatican audience.

He dislocated his right shoulder and wore a soft cast and a sling for several weeks. He blessed the faithful with his left hand and joked about an Italian report that he was suffering from amnesia and fainting spells, a report the Vatican denied.
"The Pope salutes you," he said on one occasion. "It's a slightly deficient Pope but still in one piece and not dead yet."
On April 28, 1994, when he was 73, the Pope slipped in his bath at the Vatican and broke his right femur, or thigh bone. He underwent bone replacement surgery the next day.
Despite months of physical therapy he never resumed walking with the same confidence as before the accident and often used a cane when he had to negotiate unfamiliar ground and steps.

On December 25, 1995, the world was alarmed when influenza forced the Pope to miss Christmas mass for the first time in his pontificate. Later that day nausea forced him to interrupt a televised address.
A fever which the Vatican said was of a "digestive nature" forced him to cancel public engagements in March 1996. A similar fever last August again forced him to cancel engagements.
The Vatican later said all three bouts of fever were caused by a recurring inflammation of the appendix. The discrepancies in official versions left some reporters sceptical.
